passage:
“Any bad news? I’d rather hear it today than next month,” Usha said at the team meeting.
Nobody spoke. Rohit stared at his laptop. Then Sarika said, “The figures I sent the client on Friday have a mistake. Two rows were swapped.”
“Thank you for telling me,” said Usha. “How big is it?”
“The totals are off by a bit.”
“Then we fix it today. Nobody is blamed for spotting an error.” Usha turned to the others. “I signed that file without a second check, so that is on me. From now on there are two sets of eyes on every client file.”
Sarika breathed out slowly. “I’ll write the correction email.”

qa.q: What mistake did Sarika report?
qa.a: Sarika reported that two rows in the client figures were swapped.

qa.q: Why might Sarika have hesitated before speaking?
qa.a: Sarika was probably afraid of blame for the error and of being the only one to speak, since the room was silent. The slow breath out at the end shows the tension lifted.

qa.q: Which choice by Usha made it safe to tell the truth?
qa.a: Usha thanked Sarika, said nobody is blamed for spotting an error and owned having signed without a second check. That showed bad news would be protected.

qa.q: How might Rohit, staring at his laptop, have felt when Sarika spoke?
qa.a: Rohit may have felt relieved that someone else had spoken, or worried about his own work. His silence and stare suggest tension.

grounding: Shows a leader inviting bad news, protecting the person who raises it and admitting a share of the error publicly.

passage:
At last week’s town hall, our director Payal stood and told all sixty of us that a batch of wrong labels had gone out because of her sign-off. I’m Sarita, and I’ve worked here for two years. Nobody said a word. Payal said, “I’m sorry. Here is what we are fixing, and here is who is helping.”
The room was quiet, but not the tense kind. In my old job a leader’s mistake became someone else’s fault.
Three days later a new junior found a bug in the system and reported it the same afternoon. I could see the others watching how Payal reacted. She thanked the junior by name. I felt something I hadn’t before at work: safe.

qa.q: How many people heard Payal at the town hall?
qa.a: Payal told all sixty people at the town hall.

qa.q: What did Sarita feel in the quiet room after Payal's apology?
qa.a: Sarita felt safe and trusting, unlike the tense silences in an old job. The quiet was of a different kind.

qa.q: Which choice by Payal led the junior to report the bug the same afternoon?
qa.a: Payal had owned her own mistake in public and shown who was helping. That showed the junior that admitting problems would be met with thanks, not blame.

qa.q: How might the new junior have felt reporting the bug?
qa.a: The junior was probably nervous at first, but the earlier apology made it feel possible. Being thanked by name would likely have been a relief.

grounding: Shows a leader who admits an error publicly and thanks those who raise problems, making truth safe.

passage: Ward supervisor's note, Friday. This week showed me what Francis is like as head of department. On Tuesday, Sabina, a first-year nurse, told Francis that a patient had been given the wrong diet for two days because of a labelling mix-up. She was shaking; the last nurse who reported a mistake here was moved to night shifts. Francis thanked her in front of the team. He called the patient's family himself and apologised. At Thursday's meeting he said, 'The labelling system was my responsibility. Sabina's report helped us fix it,' and asked for anyone else's concerns. Three staff raised other problems the same day. I have recommended that Francis's reporting habit be copied on other wards.

qa.q: How long had the patient been given the wrong diet?
qa.a: For two days.

qa.q: Why was Sabina shaking when she reported the mistake?
qa.a: She was afraid of punishment, since the last nurse who reported a mistake had been moved to night shifts.

qa.q: Which of Francis's actions made telling the truth safe?
qa.a: Thanking Sabina publicly, apologising to the family himself, taking responsibility for the labelling system and inviting other concerns.

qa.q: What might the three staff who raised problems be feeling?
qa.a: Safer and more trusting, encouraged to speak up after seeing Sabina protected rather than punished.

grounding: A supervisor's note on a department head who welcomes bad news, protects the junior who raised it and admits the error publicly.

passage:
Journal, Wednesday.
My first month as team lead. Today I tried something. At stand-up I said, 'Tell me the worst thing you know about our project. No blame.' Silence for a long time. Then Kiran, the newest developer, said the payment page had been failing for some customers for two weeks, and he'd been too scared to say. My first feeling was anger. I swallowed it and said, 'Thank you. That's exactly what I asked for.' Then I told the team that I had approved that release without full testing, so it was my error too. This afternoon I emailed the client to explain and apologise.
The client wasn't happy. But after the meeting, two more people came to my desk with problems they'd been hiding.
Irfan

qa.q: How long had the payment page been failing?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel when Kiran spoke up, and what did Irfan do with it?
qa.a: Irfan's first feeling was anger, which Irfan swallowed in order to thank Kiran instead.

qa.q: What steps show Irfan making truth safe?
qa.a: Inviting the worst news with no blame, thanking Kiran, admitting Irfan's own error in approving the release, and explaining honestly to the client.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt after being thanked?
qa.a: Relieved and surprised, having been too scared to speak for two weeks.

grounding: A new team lead invites bad news, protects the person who raises it and admits the lead's own error openly.

passage:
Tarun: sorry to message late. I need to tell you something about the warehouse audit
Harsha: go ahead. no rush, no blame
Tarun: I ticked 'fire extinguishers checked' last month but I didn't check all of them. 3 were expired
Harsha: thank you for telling me. are they replaced?
Tarun: not yet 😔
Harsha: ok. new ones will be delivered first thing tomorrow, and I'll stay tonight to put a warning sign on that aisle
Harsha: at tomorrow's team meeting I'll say what happened. I'll also say I never trained you properly on the audit. that's on me
Tarun: you don't have to do that
Harsha: I do. if people get punished for telling me, they'll stop telling me
Tarun: ok. thank you. I thought you'd be furious
Harsha: I'm glad you told me. that's the whole point 🙂

qa.q: How many fire extinguishers were expired?
What did Tarun expect Harsha to feel?
qa.a: Tarun feared Harsha would be furious, and feels relieved and grateful instead.

qa.q: Which steps show Harsha making it safe to report bad news?
qa.a: Thanking Tarun, acting on the risk the same night, planning to explain openly and admitting Harsha's own part in the poor training.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team react at tomorrow's meeting?
qa.a: Seeing Tarun thanked rather than punished, they are more likely to raise their own problems.

grounding: A manager welcomes a junior's admission of a safety lapse, fixes it at once and takes public responsibility.

passage: At the primary health centre in Barwani, the new medical officer, Dr Vijay Patil, began every Monday with the same question: "What went wrong last week?" For a month nobody answered. Then Mehak, the youngest nurse, raised her hand. "Sir, two vaccine boxes sat outside the fridge on Friday, because the power went and nobody switched on the generator." The room froze. Under the old officer, that meant a written warning. Dr Patil wrote it on the board. "Thank you, Mehak. That's exactly what I need to know." Then, in front of everyone: "And it's my fault. I never told anyone the generator was their job." He named the ward attendant in charge, set an alarm schedule, and sent the two boxes to the district store for checking. At the next Monday meeting, three people spoke up.

qa.q: What question did Dr Patil ask every Monday?
qa.a: "What went wrong last week?"

qa.q: What was Mehak probably feeling when she raised her hand?
qa.a: She was likely nervous, fearing the written warning the old officer would have given, but felt responsible for the boxes.

qa.q: Which of Dr Patil's actions made telling the truth feel safe?
qa.a: He thanked Mehak publicly, admitted his own fault, then fixed the process and sent the boxes for checking instead of punishing anyone.

qa.q: Why might three people have spoken up at the next meeting?
qa.a: They saw that bad news brought thanks and fixes, not blame, so they felt safe enough to share their own problems.

grounding: Shows a leader inviting bad news, thanking the nurse who raised it and admitting his own error, which builds trust.
